questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Function on Which to Apply a Root-Finding Method When Applying the Trapezoidal Method
questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2x{y}^{2},\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2x{y}^{2}+2{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2})\cdot 1 \\  & =x{y}^{2}+{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+x{y}^{2}+{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-y-x{y}^{2}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-y-x{y}^{2}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-2({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-1-1(1)^{2} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-2({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2x\sqrt{y},\,y(0)=3
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **general form** of $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ in terms of the new values ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and the current values $x$ and $y?$
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2x\sqrt{y}+2{x}_{\text{new}}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}})\cdot 1 \\  & =x\sqrt{y}+{x}_{\text{new}}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+x\sqrt{y}+{x}_{\text{new}}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{{{y}_{\text{new}}-{x}_{\text{new}}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-x\sqrt{y}}_{⏟}}_{g({y}_{\text{new}})}=0.
$$

Therefore, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-{x}_{\text{new}}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-x\sqrt{y}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x-2\sqrt{y},\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-2\sqrt{y}+{x}_{\text{new}}-2\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}})\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}-\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}-\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{\text{new}}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

 Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}(1)-\frac{1}{2}(2)+1+\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}-1+1+\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}+\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x-{y}^{3},\,y(0)=1
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(1).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(1)≈$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=1-0=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((x-{y}^{3})+({x}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}))\cdot 1 \\  & =0.5x-0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5x-0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5x=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5x.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1.
$$

 Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5(1)^{3}-1-0.5\cdot 1-0.5\cdot 0 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=1.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-1}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =0.8 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈0.771\,429 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈0.770\,917\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈0.77,$ rounded to two decimal places.

$$

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$

$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=1-0=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((1-x{y}^{2})+(1-{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}))\cdot 1 \\  & =1-0.5x{y}^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+1-0.5x{y}^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-1+0.5x{y}^{2}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-1+0.5x{y}^{2}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1.
$$

Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5(1)({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1-1+0.5(0)(1)^{2} \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=({y}_{\text{new}})+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-2}{({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}+1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =1.25 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.236\,111 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.236\,068\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈1.24,$ rounded to two decimal places.
